newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Ariane to cut costs in face of U.S challenge.
newsitem.headline: Ariane to cut costs in face of U.S challenge.

text.p: Western Europe's satellite launch company Arianespace said on Monday it planned to cut costs in the face of growing competition from merging U.S. companies.

The Paris-based firm that controls over half the world's commercial rocket market fears its lead is threatened by American consolidation -- notably the planned purchase of McDonnell Douglas Corp by Boeing.

"The reduction of (Ariane's) cost is a major, vital objective. We must reduce the costs of (rocket) manufacture and launching our rockets," Roger Solari, French Guiana operations director for Arianespace, told a news conference.

Link-ups among U.S. companies "will lead to the lowering of space transport costs," he said. Solari said Ariane was working to cut the time needed to prepare each rocket, to allow more launches and was stressing launch of heavier satellite payloads.
"We have to deal with two new giants in the space transport world. This is the association of Lockheed Martin -Loral and the association of Boeing-McDonnell Douglas-Rockwell," he said.
"These are two market giants that have come onto the market with considerable products and join the launching of satellites and the manufacture of satellites," he said.
Arianespace launches the Ariane-4 rocket series from the European Space Agency (ESA) launch centre in Kourou, French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America.

It successfully launched 15 satellites aboard 10 Ariane-4 rockets in 1996 and signed firm contracts during the year for the launch of 19 more satellites that brings its satellite launch orders to 42, worth an estimated $3.5 billion.
But on June 4, the first new generation Ariane-5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after its maiden launch in a major setback for the European space programme.

Arianespace was scheduled to take over commercial operations of Ariane-5 early this year -- but the new rocket's commercial future is now in doubt and a second experimental launch of the more powerful rocket is now planned for July at earliest.

Boeing's planned purchase of McDonnell Douglas will give the new company a slice of the Sea Launch satellite system being prepared for its maiden flight in 1998 using a Russian Zenit rocket launched from an offshore drilling platform in the Pacific Ocean. Boeing has a 40 percent stake in the project.
It will also hand it McDonnell Douglas' flight-proven Delta family of rockets, used to launch satellites from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Lockheed Martin controls the International Launch Services (ILS) company that launches the Atlas and Russia's Proton rocket.
Specialists said major satellite launch companies had underestimated the demand for their services in the early 1990s, particularly from booming markets in the Asia-Pacific region.
